title: Mambo Italiano
full_review:
The comedy "Mambo Italiano" (Goldwyn) strains to be funny and touching as the derivative script mixes stereotypical ethnic characters with gay life issues.

Set in Canada -- specifically in Montreal's Little Italy -- the predictable film, directed by Emile Gaudreault, tells the story of Angelo (Luke Kirby), a young man browbeaten by his traditional Italian immigrant parents, Maria (Ginette Reno) and Gino (Paul Sorvino). Aspiring to be a television writer but stuck in a dull job, Angelo is also struggling with his sexuality.

The first blow to his tight-knit family, which includes wacky sister Anna (Claudia Ferri), is Angelo's announcement that he is moving out. "What's so wrong with living with your parents until you get married?" protest his parents. They are momentarily relieved when Angelo's childhood friend, Nino (Peter Miller), a respectable cop, moves in with him. But their relief is short-lived when they discover that Angelo and Nino are actually lovers.

Gaudreault's film walks a fine line between approval of the gay lifestyle and acceptance of the homosexual person. It is realistic in portraying the reaction of Angelo's parents to the news that he is gay: horror, indignation, sorrow and, finally, a loving resignation to their son's sexuality and recognition that Angelo will always be their son no matter what. However, the movie openly portrays Angelo and Nino's relationship, which is likely to be troubling to Catholic viewers. It exposes their growth, both as a couple and as individuals, for laughs, lacking any insight or sensitivity.

"Mambo" plays like a poor man's gay version of "My Big Fat Greek Wedding" except that the good-natured "Wedding" was far cleverer and treated its characters with affection. In one scene from "Mambo," a resentful and insolent Angelo lets loose on his parents with a torrent of accusations and insults that would turn the stomach of any parent in the audience. The force and intensity of the scene is out of step with the film's otherwise farcical tone. "Mambo's" colorful and purposely gaudy costumes and set designs recall Baz Luhrmann's 1993 "Strictly Ballroom" and cheerily juxtapose with the sometimes gloomy outlook of the characters.

Although the long-winded script is flawed with holes that a Mack truck could comfortably ride through, the film eventually ends on an up note, showing itself to be a movie about familial forgiveness and acceptance of oneself and others, imperfections included.
Because of a few instances of same-sex kissing and implied sexual encounters with intermittent rough language and profanity, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-IV -- adults, with reservations. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
